prompt: Which of these can a stand-in give a test that the real payment provider cannot?
hint: Think of the four reasons the section gives.

choices.text: Proof that the provider still answers the way it did last month
choices.why: That is exactly what a stand-in cannot prove: it answers what somebody wrote.

choices.text: A decline whenever the test asks for one
choices.why: Right. Failures on demand are the main reason to replace a dependency.

choices.text: Real charges, so the money flow is tested end to end
choices.why: A stand-in moves no money; avoiding real charges is one of the reasons to use it.

choices.text: A sandbox with test cards
choices.why: Sandboxes are offered by real providers, on their servers and their terms.

prompt: Match each kind of test double to what it does.
hint: One of them works; one of them can fail the test on its own.

pairs.right: answers with what it was told to answer
answers, and records what it received for the test to read
holds expectations and fails the test if the calls do not arrive
a simplified implementation that really works

right_distractors: a copy of the provider's production database

prompt: A colleague tests boxoffice by replacing the payment provider and also the function in boxoffice that checks the provider's status code. What is wrong with that?
hint: Where does the line go?

choices.text: Nothing; the more is replaced, the faster and steadier the test
choices.why: Speed is not the point once the test no longer runs the code it claims to test.

choices.text: The provider should be the real sandbox instead
choices.why: Using the sandbox or a stand-in for the provider is a separate choice; the problem is inside boxoffice.

choices.text: That part of boxoffice is no longer tested
choices.why: Right. Replace what lies outside the boundary and nothing inside it.

choices.text: A stand-in may only replace a server, never a function
choices.why: Test doubles started as objects in unit tests; the rule is about the boundary, not the kind of thing.

prompt: An order was placed without an Idempotency-Key header. Which idempotency key did boxoffice send to the stub?
hint: Look at GET /__requests, or at `key || id` in boxoffice's code.

choices.text: None; the header was left out
choices.why: boxoffice always sends one; without the client's key it uses its own value.

choices.text: A random UUID made for the charge
choices.why: Nothing in boxoffice makes a UUID; the value is predictable.

choices.text: The token's client id, ci-tests
choices.why: The client id scopes the remembered replies inside boxoffice; it is not sent to the provider.

choices.text: The order's id, ord-1001
choices.why: Right. `key || id` falls back to the order id, which is also the reference.

prompt: Why does the stub exit at start-up when MODE is "declined" instead of starting in approve mode?
hint: What would a test that expects a decline see otherwise?

choices.text: A typo would approve every charge, so the decline test tests nothing
choices.why: Right. A silent fallback turns a typo into a green test.

choices.text: Node cannot read environment variables after the server starts listening
choices.why: Node reads them at any time; the check is placed before listen on purpose.

choices.text: Port 8090 is reserved for the approve mode
choices.why: The port does not depend on the mode.

choices.text: boxoffice refuses to talk to a stub in an unknown mode
choices.why: boxoffice never learns the stub's mode; it only sees the answers.

prompt: Match each stub mode to the status boxoffice answers the order with.
hint: Two of them come from lesson 13's subject, the error path.

prompt: An order of six seats of sh-101 (48000 cents) matches both mapping files. Why does WireMock answer with the decline?
hint: Look at the field the two files set differently.

choices.text: The decline file comes first in alphabetical order
choices.why: WireMock does not choose by file name; without priorities it prefers the most recently added.

choices.text: Its priority is 1, and the lower number wins
choices.why: Right. The approve file has priority 5.

choices.text: The approve file requires a Content-Type that boxoffice does not send
choices.why: boxoffice sends application/json, which the approve file accepts.

choices.text: WireMock always picks the mapping with the most conditions
choices.why: The near-miss report even picked the one with fewer conditions as closest; priority decides between matches.

prompt: A test against WireMock fails because a charge got a 404. What should you read first?
hint: WireMock explains its own 404.

choices.text: boxoffice's log, which shows the 404 line
choices.why: boxoffice only logs its own answer; it does not know why WireMock refused.

choices.text: The provider's documentation, to see what its 404 status means for a charge
choices.why: The real provider was never asked; the 404 came from the stand-in.

choices.text: The body of the 404: the closest mapping and the difference
choices.why: Right. The line marked <<<<< usually names the one thing to fix.

choices.text: WireMock's start-up lines, to check the port
choices.why: A wrong port gives a refused connection, not a 404 from WireMock.

prompt: After the journal was emptied and boxoffice placed its two orders, what count did /__admin/requests/count give for POST /charges?
hint: One charge per order.

prompt: In a WireMock mapping, the field that picks between two mappings that both match is called ___.
hint: The lower number wins.

prompt: Prism answers GET /v1/shows/sh-999 with a show. Why?
hint: What does the contract say, and what does it not say?

choices.text: boxoffice's contract lists sh-999 among its examples
choices.why: The only example id is sh-103, which is what Prism sent back.

choices.text: The contract describes what a show looks like, not which shows exist
choices.why: Right. Prism builds the answer from the schema and has no list to refuse with.

choices.text: Prism forwards the request to boxoffice on port 8080
choices.why: In mock mode Prism forwards nothing; that is the proxy mode of section 06.

choices.text: A 404 is not declared for that path
choices.why: The contract does declare a 404 there; Prism still had no way to know sh-999 is missing.

prompt: Which of these did the Prism mock refuse, where the real boxoffice answered without refusing?
hint: Two requests, and lesson 2 found both.

choices.text: An order with an extra field, seat_class
choices.why: Right. The contract's NewOrder forbids additional properties; boxoffice created the order.

choices.text: The list of shows with date=tomorrow
choices.why: Right. Prism answered 400; boxoffice answered 200 with an empty list.

choices.text: An order of seven seats
choices.why: Both refuse seven seats with 422; there they agree.

choices.text: A token for a client called nobody
choices.why: Prism gave nobody a token; it was boxoffice that would refuse it with 401.

prompt: Who gains most from a Prism mock of boxoffice?
hint: Who calls boxoffice?

choices.text: boxoffice's own tester, who can stop starting the server
choices.why: Testing a mock of boxoffice tests the contract's examples, not boxoffice.

choices.text: The payment provider, which can check boxoffice's charges
choices.why: The provider is on the other side; Prism here stands in for boxoffice itself.

choices.text: A team building a client, such as the Tickets app
choices.why: Right. They can work before boxoffice exists and ask for any status with Prefer.

choices.text: The theatre's staff reading the sales report
choices.why: Staff need the real numbers; Prism invents zeros.

prompt: A WireMock mapping answers a charge with 200, and every order through boxoffice fails with 502. Which program is wrong?
hint: Neither program can settle it.

choices.text: boxoffice, because 200 means the charge worked
choices.why: 200 is a success code, but what this provider answers is fixed by its contract, which says 201.

choices.text: The mapping: the provider's contract says 201
choices.why: Right. Who is right is decided by what the provider promises.

choices.text: Neither: a 502 is the provider's outage
choices.why: No provider was called; WireMock answered at once.

choices.text: WireMock itself, which cannot send 200 to Node's fetch
choices.why: WireMock sent 200 and boxoffice read it; the log says payments answered 200.

prompt: What does Prism do in proxy mode with --errors?
hint: It answers nothing itself.

choices.text: Answers from the contract's examples, like the mock
choices.why: That is mock mode; a proxy forwards to a real server.

choices.text: Records the real server's answers into mapping files
choices.why: That is recording, a different tool's feature; Prism checks, it does not write mappings.

choices.text: Forwards, checks both ways, and reports a violation as an error
choices.why: Right. The 200 came back as a 500 with sl-violations.

choices.text: Retries the request until the server answers as the contract says
choices.why: It never retries; it reports.

prompt: Your stand-in was written by reading your own client code and copying what it expects. Why does a referee check matter even more then?
hint: What does a stand-in written from your code agree with?

choices.text: Copied stand-ins are slower, so timeouts appear
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with where the answers came from.

choices.text: Prism cannot read stand-ins written by hand
choices.why: Prism checks answers on the wire; it never reads the stand-in's code.

choices.text: Client code is always right about the provider, so the check finds nothing
choices.why: If the client were always right, the 200 example would never happen.

choices.text: It agrees with your code by construction, so every test passes even when both are wrong
choices.why: Right. Only the provider's contract is outside the two.

prompt: The Tickets team built the app against the Prism mock of boxoffice, and every screen worked. In production, a user who picks a malformed date sees "no shows that day" instead of an error. What happened?
hint: Compare what the mock and boxoffice answered for date=tomorrow.

choices.text: The mock lost the date on the way, so the app sent none
choices.why: The mock answered 400 to the date it received; nothing was lost.

choices.text: The mock followed the contract's 400; boxoffice answers 200 with an empty list
choices.why: Right. The app's error screen was built for an answer boxoffice never gives.

choices.text: The app cached the mock's list of one show
choices.why: The symptom is an empty list from the server, not a cached one.

choices.text: Prism was started without --errors, so it accepted the date
choices.why: The mock refused the date with 400 without --errors; that flag belongs to the proxy section.

prompt: Put the steps of section 06 in order, from writing the lie to catching it.
hint: The referee needs the contract before it can judge anything.
items: add a mapping answering 200 through WireMock's admin API
place an order and see boxoffice answer 502
start Prism in proxy mode in front of WireMock
send a charge through the proxy and read sl-violations

prompt: You need a test that checks boxoffice charges 48000 cents for six seats of sh-101. Which stand-in setup lets the test assert that?
hint: The assertion is about what boxoffice sent, not what it got back.

choices.text: A Prism mock of boxoffice's own contract
choices.why: That replaces boxoffice, the thing under test, and the order would be invented.

choices.text: A stub that only answers 201 approved and records nothing
choices.why: It would let the order through, but nothing would show the amount it received.

choices.text: A spy, read after the order: WireMock's journal or /__requests
choices.why: Right. A stand-in that records is what makes the amount observable.

choices.text: The real provider's sandbox, whose receipts list the amount of every charge it took
choices.why: The sandbox shows its own view on its own terms; the test cannot read it the way it reads a spy.

prompt: Which of these would a Prism proxy in front of the stub report as a violation of payments.yaml?
hint: Read the three things the contract says, and that it lists no 500.

choices.text: The stub in down mode answering 500
choices.why: Right. The contract lists only 201, so any other status is reported.

choices.text: The stub in decline mode answering 201 declined
choices.why: declined is one of the two allowed statuses; that answer follows the contract.

choices.text: A charge sent without the idempotency-key header
choices.why: Right. The proxy checks requests too, and the header is required.

choices.text: boxoffice's charge for 16000 cents with reference ord-1001
choices.why: Both required fields are there with the right types.
